Proverbs.line: Proverbs gathers wise sayings, mostly from Solomon, teaching that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.
more: Chapters 1–9 are a father's appeals to his son to embrace wisdom and avoid folly and adultery.
Wisdom and Folly are pictured as two women inviting the simple to their houses.
Chapters 10–22 collect short proverbs of Solomon contrasting the righteous and the wicked, the wise and the fool.
Further collections follow: sayings of the wise, Solomon's proverbs copied by Hezekiah's men, and words of Agur and Lemuel.
The book closes with a poem praising the excellent wife who fears the LORD.

1.line: The book states its purpose, a father warns his son against violent sinners, and Wisdom cries out in the streets.
more: Proverbs aims to give prudence to the simple and understanding to the wise.
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom.
Wisdom warns that those who refuse her call will face calamity without help.

2.line: The father teaches that seeking wisdom like treasure brings understanding of the fear of the LORD and protection from evil.
more: Wisdom guards from men of perverse speech who walk in darkness.
It also delivers from the forbidden woman whose house leads down to death.
The upright will dwell in the land, but the wicked will be cut off.

3.line: The son is urged to trust the LORD wholeheartedly, honor him, accept his discipline, and treasure wisdom above riches.
more: The LORD disciplines those he loves as a father does a son.
Wisdom is more precious than jewels, a tree of life to those who hold her.
The LORD founded the earth by wisdom.
The son should do good to neighbors and not envy the violent.

4.line: A father passes on his own father's teaching: get wisdom, keep to the righteous path, and guard your heart.
more: The path of the righteous grows brighter, while the way of the wicked is deep darkness.
The son must keep his speech honest, his eyes forward, and his feet from evil.

5.line: The father warns against the adulteress, whose words are smooth but whose end is bitter and leads to death.
more: Going to her squanders strength, wealth, and honor, ending in regret.
The son is urged to rejoice in the wife of his youth.
The LORD sees every path, and the wicked are caught by their own sins.

6.line: Warnings are given against rash pledges, laziness, troublemakers, and adultery, along with seven things the LORD hates.
more: One who has guaranteed a neighbor's debt should hurry to be freed.
The sluggard is told to learn diligence from the ant.
The LORD hates pride, lies, violence, wicked plans, false witness, and sowing discord.
Adultery brings wounds, disgrace, and a jealous husband's fury.

7.line: The father describes a simple young man lured by an adulterous woman into her house, like an ox to slaughter.
more: The son is told to keep the father's commands and call wisdom his sister.
The woman meets the youth at twilight with seductive words while her husband is away.
Her house is the way to Sheol and the chambers of death.

8.line: Wisdom calls out publicly, describing her worth, her role in just rule, and her presence with the LORD at creation.
more: Her words are righteous and more valuable than silver, gold, or jewels.
By wisdom kings reign and rulers decree what is just.
She was beside the LORD before the world began, rejoicing in his work.
Whoever finds her finds life; whoever misses her harms himself.

9.line: Wisdom and Folly, pictured as two women, each invite the simple to a feast, with opposite results.
more: Wisdom builds her house, prepares a meal, and offers life and insight.
Correcting a scoffer brings abuse, but rebuking a wise man makes him wiser.
Folly is loud and ignorant; her guests end up in the depths of Sheol.

10.line: Solomon's collection of short proverbs begins, contrasting the righteous and the wicked in work, wealth, and speech.
more: A wise son brings joy, but a foolish son brings grief.
Diligent hands bring wealth, while laziness brings poverty.
Restrained, truthful speech is wise, while many words invite sin.
The fear of the LORD prolongs life, but the years of the wicked are cut short.

11.line: Proverbs contrast honesty and deceit, humility and pride, generosity and greed, and the destinies of righteous and wicked.
more: The LORD hates false scales but delights in honest weights.
Righteousness delivers from death, while riches do not help in the day of wrath.
The generous person prospers, and whoever trusts in riches will fall.
A city rejoices when the righteous prosper and is overthrown by the words of the wicked.

12.line: Proverbs contrast the wise who accept correction with fools, and truthful speech and diligence with lies and laziness.
more: Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but one who hates reproof is stupid.
An excellent wife is her husband's crown.
Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, while truthful lips endure.
The diligent will rule, while slothfulness leads to forced labor.

13.line: Proverbs address guarding speech, accepting instruction, diligent work, honest wealth, and wise companions.
more: Whoever guards his mouth preserves his life.
Wealth gained hastily dwindles, but gathering little by little increases it.
Walking with the wise makes one wise, while companions of fools suffer harm.
Whoever spares the rod hates his son.

14.line: Proverbs contrast wise and foolish living, highlighting the fear of the LORD, self-control, and kindness to the poor.
more: The wise woman builds her house, but folly tears it down.
There is a way that seems right but ends in death.
A tranquil heart gives life, while envy rots the bones.
Oppressing the poor insults their Maker, while kindness to the needy honors him.

15.line: Proverbs highlight gentle speech, the LORD's watchful eyes, contentment with little, and the value of counsel.
more: A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs anger.
The eyes of the LORD are everywhere, watching evil and good.
Better a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure with trouble.
Plans fail without counsel but succeed with many advisers.

16.line: Proverbs emphasize the LORD's sovereignty over human plans, the value of righteousness, and the danger of pride.
more: People make plans, but the LORD directs their steps.
Kings should rule in righteousness, and honest weights belong to the LORD.
Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.
Gray hair is a crown gained in a righteous life.

17.line: Proverbs address peace in the home, faithful friendship, justice, foolish talk, and the value of restraint.
more: Better a dry morsel with quiet than a house of feasting full of strife.
A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
A joyful heart is good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries the bones.
Even a fool who keeps silent is considered wise.

18.line: Proverbs address isolation, the power of the tongue, the safety found in the LORD, and the value of hearing both sides.
more: The name of the LORD is a strong tower for the righteous.
Death and life are in the power of the tongue.
The first to plead seems right until another examines him.
Whoever finds a wife finds a good thing and favor from the LORD.

19.line: Proverbs address integrity in poverty, false witnesses, patience, family life, and the LORD's purpose prevailing over human plans.
more: Better a poor man with integrity than a crooked fool.
A false witness will not go unpunished.
A prudent wife is from the LORD.
Many plans are in a person's heart, but the LORD's purpose stands.

20.line: Proverbs warn against wine, laziness, dishonest scales, and revenge, and note that the LORD searches the human spirit.
more: Wine is a mocker and strong drink a brawler.
Unequal weights and measures are both an abomination to the LORD.
Do not repay evil, but wait for the LORD to deliver.
The human spirit is the lamp of the LORD, searching the inner parts.

21.line: Proverbs teach that the LORD directs kings' hearts and prefers righteousness and justice to sacrifice.
more: The king's heart is like streams of water in the LORD's hand.
Better to live in a corner of the roof than with a quarrelsome wife.
Whoever closes his ear to the poor will himself go unheard.
No wisdom or plan succeeds against the LORD, who gives the victory.

22.line: Solomon's collection closes with proverbs on reputation and training children, and the sayings of the wise begin.
more: A good name is better than great riches.
A child should be trained in the way he should go.
The sayings of the wise warn against robbing the poor, befriending hotheads, and moving ancient landmarks.

23.line: The sayings of the wise warn against gluttony, chasing riches, and drunkenness, and urge listening to parents.
more: One should be careful at a ruler's table and not wear oneself out for wealth.
Discipline should not be withheld from a child.
Do not envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD.
The drunkard is described as dazed, bruised, and still wanting more wine.

24.line: The sayings of the wise warn against envying evildoers, urge rescuing the endangered, and commend justice and diligence.
more: A house is built by wisdom and established by understanding.
Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, or fret over evildoers.
A further set of sayings condemns partiality in judgment and false witness.
A neglected field shows how a little sleep brings poverty.

25.line: A collection of Solomon's proverbs copied by Hezekiah's men begins, addressing kings, humility, wise speech, and kindness to enemies.
more: It is God's glory to conceal things and kings' glory to search them out.
Do not exalt yourself before the king; wait to be invited higher.
A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in silver.
Feeding a hungry enemy heaps burning coals on his head.

26.line: Proverbs describe the fool, the sluggard, the meddler, and the deceiver, showing the harm each causes.
more: Honor does not fit a fool, and answering him requires discernment.
The sluggard turns on his bed like a door on its hinges.
Gossip fuels quarrels as wood feeds a fire.
Hatred hidden by smooth words will be exposed, and the schemer falls into his own pit.

27.line: Proverbs address boasting about tomorrow, faithful friendship, mutual sharpening, and careful attention to one's flocks.
more: Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what it brings.
Faithful are the wounds of a friend.
As iron sharpens iron, one person sharpens another.
Know the condition of your flocks, for riches do not last forever.

28.line: Proverbs contrast the bold righteous with the fleeing wicked, focusing on the law, just rulers, confession, and honest gain.
more: The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as lions.
Whoever conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses finds mercy.
A wicked ruler over poor people is like a charging bear.
One hasty to be rich will not go unpunished.

29.line: Proverbs address stubbornness, righteous and wicked rulers, discipline of children, anger, and the need for prophetic vision.
more: When the righteous increase, the people rejoice; when the wicked rule, they groan.
The rod and reproof give wisdom.
Where there is no prophetic vision, the people cast off restraint.
The fear of man is a snare, but trusting the LORD brings safety.

30.line: Agur confesses his limited understanding, prays for neither poverty nor riches, and gives numerical sayings about the world.
more: Every word of God proves true, and nothing should be added to his words.
Agur asks to be kept from falsehood, poverty, and riches.
His numerical sayings list things never satisfied, things too wonderful to understand, and small but wise creatures.

31.line: King Lemuel records his mother's counsel on just rule, and the book closes with a poem praising the excellent wife.
more: Lemuel's mother warns against women and wine and urges defending the poor and needy.
The excellent wife is trustworthy, industrious, generous, wise, and strong.
Charm is deceitful and beauty fleeting, but a woman who fears the LORD is praised.

Ecclesiastes.line: The Preacher, son of David, explores life under the sun and concludes that everything is vanity apart from fearing God.
more: He tests wisdom, pleasure, and great works, finding none of them lasting or satisfying.
He observes injustice, oppression, and death, which fall on wise and foolish alike.
He counsels enjoying food, work, and family as God's gifts while revering God.
He urges remembering the Creator in youth, before old age and death.
The conclusion is to fear God and keep his commandments, for God will judge every deed.

1.line: The Preacher declares all things vanity and finds that endless cycles of nature and human striving gain nothing lasting.
more: Generations come and go while the sun, wind, and rivers repeat their courses.
There is nothing new under the sun, and past things are forgotten.
He set out to study everything by wisdom and found it a striving after wind.

2.line: The Preacher tests pleasure, great projects, and wisdom, and finds them all vanity, since death comes to wise and fool alike.
more: He built houses, planted vineyards, gathered wealth, and denied himself no pleasure.
Wisdom excels folly, yet both the wise and the fool die and are forgotten.
He hated his toil, since he must leave its fruit to another.
Eating, drinking, and finding enjoyment in work are from the hand of God.

3.line: There is a time for everything under heaven, and God has made all things beautiful in their time.
more: God has put eternity into human hearts, yet they cannot grasp his whole work.
What God does endures forever, so that people fear before him.
Wickedness sits in the place of justice, but God will judge the righteous and the wicked.
Humans and beasts alike die and return to dust.

4.line: The Preacher observes oppression, envious toil, and lonely striving, and finds companionship better than isolation.
more: The oppressed have no comforter, and the dead seem better off than the living.
Much toil springs from envy, yet idleness is also folly.
Two are better than one, and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
A poor wise youth is better than an old foolish king, yet popularity fades.

5.line: The Preacher urges reverence and few words before God, warns against rash vows, and shows the emptiness of loving money.
more: It is better not to vow than to vow and not pay.
Whoever loves money is never satisfied with it.
People leave the world naked, carrying nothing from their toil.
Enjoying one's lot and wealth as God's gift is good and fitting.

6.line: The Preacher laments those who have wealth and long life but cannot enjoy them, and asks what is truly good.
more: A stillborn child is better off than one who lives long without satisfaction.
All human toil is for the mouth, yet the appetite is never filled.
No one can contend with God or know what will come after him.

7.line: The Preacher offers proverbs on sorrow, patience, and moderation, and finds that no one is righteous and wisdom is elusive.
more: The day of death is better than the day of birth, and mourning better than feasting.
In prosperity be joyful, and in adversity consider that God made both.
There is not a righteous man on earth who never sins.
God made humanity upright, but they have sought out many schemes.

8.line: The Preacher counsels obedience to the king and observes that the wicked go unpunished, yet those who fear God will fare well.
more: No one has power over the day of death.
Because sentence is not executed quickly, people are bent on evil.
He commends joy, since no one can fully discover God's work under the sun.

9.line: The same fate of death comes to all, so the Preacher urges enjoying life now and values wisdom though it is overlooked.
more: The living know they will die, while the dead know nothing under the sun.
Eat with joy, enjoy life with your wife, and work with all your might.
The race is not always to the swift, for time and chance happen to all.
A poor wise man saved a city, yet no one remembered him.

10.line: Proverbs show how a little folly outweighs wisdom, and address foolish rulers, careless work, idle talk, and laziness.
more: Dead flies make perfume stink, and a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.
Fools are sometimes set in high places while the worthy sit low.
A fool multiplies words, and laziness lets the roof sag.
Do not curse the king, even in your thoughts.

11.line: The Preacher urges bold, generous work despite an uncertain future and tells the young to rejoice while remembering God's judgment.
more: Cast your bread upon the waters and give a portion to many.
Whoever watches the wind will not sow, so sow in morning and evening.
Youth should enjoy its days, knowing God will bring them into judgment.

12.line: The Preacher urges remembering the Creator in youth before old age and death, then concludes: fear God and keep his commandments.
more: Old age is pictured as a failing house, ending with dust returning to the earth.
The spirit returns to God who gave it.
The Preacher taught knowledge and arranged many proverbs with care.
God will bring every deed into judgment, including every secret thing.

Song of Solomon.line: Solomon's Song is a love poem celebrating the desire, delight, and commitment between a bride and her beloved.
more: The bride and groom express longing and praise in alternating speeches, with the women of Jerusalem as a chorus.
Their courtship moves through meetings, separations, and searches in the city.
A royal wedding procession and the consummation of their love occur at the center.
After a time of distance, they are reunited and praise each other again.
The song closes declaring love as strong as death and unquenchable.

1.line: The bride longs for her beloved, describes herself as dark but lovely, and the two exchange words of praise.
more: She asks where her beloved pastures his flock at noon.
He compares her to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots and praises her beauty.
The daughters of Jerusalem respond to the bride as a chorus.

2.line: The lovers delight in each other, the bride urges patience in love, and her beloved invites her out in springtime.
more: She is a lily among brambles, and he is an apple tree among trees.
She charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love until it pleases.
He calls her to come away, for winter is past.
She declares that her beloved is hers and she is his.

3.line: The bride searches the city at night and finds her beloved, then Solomon's wedding procession approaches.
more: She seeks him on her bed and in the streets, then holds him fast when found.
Solomon arrives in a carriage escorted by sixty mighty men.
The daughters of Zion are called to see him crowned on his wedding day.

4.line: The groom praises his bride's beauty in detail and invites her to come with him, and she invites him into her garden.
more: He describes her eyes, hair, teeth, lips, and neck with images from nature.
He calls her flawless and says she has captivated his heart.
He pictures her as a locked garden and a sealed fountain.

5.line: After the groom comes to his garden, the bride hesitates to open to him at night, then searches for him in distress.
more: When she opens, he has gone, and the watchmen beat her.
The daughters of Jerusalem ask what makes her beloved better than others.
She describes his appearance in detail and calls him her friend.

6.line: The bride says her beloved has gone to his garden, and he praises her as unique among queens and concubines.
more: She affirms that she belongs to her beloved and he to her.
He calls her beautiful as Tirzah and awesome as an army with banners.
She is his one perfect dove, praised even by queens.

7.line: The groom praises his bride's beauty from feet to head, and she invites him to the fields to give her love.
more: He compares her stature to a palm tree and longs to climb it.
She declares that his desire is for her.
She invites him to the villages and vineyards in spring.

8.line: The bride wishes for open affection, declares love strong as death, and the song ends with the lovers calling to each other.
more: She asks to be set as a seal upon his heart.
Many waters cannot quench love, and it cannot be bought.
Her brothers speak of their little sister, and she compares her vineyard to Solomon's.

Isaiah.line: Isaiah prophesies judgment on Judah and the nations and promises salvation through the LORD's servant and a renewed Zion.
more: Chapters 1–12 indict Judah's sin and promise a remnant and a coming Davidic king called Immanuel.
Chapters 13–35 announce oracles against the nations and the LORD's final judgment and restoration.
Chapters 36–39 narrate Jerusalem's deliverance from Assyria and Hezekiah's illness and folly with Babylon.
Chapters 40–55 comfort Israel with promises of return from Babylon and the Servant's atoning suffering.
Chapters 56–66 call for true righteousness and foresee new heavens, a new earth, and final judgment.

1.line: The LORD charges Judah with rebellion and empty worship, calls them to repent, and promises Zion's purging and restoration.
more: The nation is like a beaten body, and Jerusalem is left like a lonely booth.
God rejects their sacrifices and festivals because their hands are full of blood.
Though their sins are like scarlet, they can be made white as snow.
Rebels will be destroyed, but Zion will be redeemed by justice.

2.line: Isaiah foresees nations streaming to the LORD's exalted mountain, then announces a day when proud humanity will be brought low.
more: Nations will learn God's ways and beat swords into plowshares.
Judah is full of foreign practices, wealth, and idols.
On the day of the LORD, the proud are humbled and idols discarded.
People will hide in caves from the terror of the LORD.

3.line: The LORD announces that Jerusalem's leaders will be removed and the proud daughters of Zion humbled for their oppression.
more: Support will be taken away, leaving children and incompetent rulers in charge.
The LORD rises to judge elders and princes who crushed the poor.
The haughty women's finery will be replaced with rags, and their men will fall in war.

4.line: After judgment, the LORD will cleanse Zion and cover it with his glory, and the Branch of the LORD will flourish.
more: Seven women will seek one man to remove their disgrace.
The survivors in Jerusalem will be called holy.
A cloud by day and fire by night will shelter Zion.

5.line: Isaiah's song of the vineyard pictures Israel as yielding wild grapes, followed by woes and a coming invasion.
more: The LORD will remove his vineyard's protection because it produced injustice instead of justice.
Woes fall on land-grabbers, drunkards, scoffers, and those who call evil good.
The LORD will summon a distant nation that comes swiftly to devour.

6.line: Isaiah sees the LORD enthroned in the temple, is cleansed of his sin, and is sent to a hardened people.
more: Seraphim call out that the LORD of hosts is holy.
A seraph touches Isaiah's lips with a burning coal to atone for his sin.
He is told the people will not understand until the land lies desolate.
A holy seed will remain like a stump.

7.line: Isaiah urges King Ahaz to trust God against Syria and Israel and gives the sign of Immanuel born of a virgin.
more: Isaiah and his son meet Ahaz, assuring him the alliance against Judah will fail.
Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign, yet the LORD gives one.
Matthew applies the virgin-born Immanuel prophecy to Jesus.
Assyria will later devastate Judah's land.

8.line: Isaiah's son's name signals Assyria's coming invasion, and the prophet is told to fear the LORD rather than conspiracies.
more: Maher-shalal-hash-baz is born as a sign that Damascus and Samaria will be plundered.
Assyria will sweep into Judah like a flooding river.
The LORD will be a sanctuary to some and a stumbling stone to others.
People should seek the law and the testimony, not mediums.

9.line: Isaiah promises light to Galilee through a child born to rule on David's throne, then announces judgment on proud Israel.
more: The child will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.
His government and peace will have no end.
Matthew applies the light dawning in Galilee to Jesus' ministry.
Israel's arrogance brings repeated judgments, yet the LORD's anger is not turned away.

10.line: Woe is pronounced on unjust lawmakers, and Assyria, God's rod of judgment, will itself be punished for its arrogance.
more: Assyria boasts of its own strength, not knowing God is using it.
The LORD will consume Assyria's glory like fire in a forest.
A remnant of Israel will return to the Mighty God.
The Assyrian advance on Jerusalem will be cut down like trees.

11.line: A shoot from Jesse's stump will rule in righteousness by the Spirit, bringing peace and regathering God's scattered people.
more: The Spirit of wisdom, counsel, and the fear of the LORD rests on him.
The wolf will dwell with the lamb, and the earth will be full of God's knowledge.
Nations will seek him, and Israel's exiles will return as in the Exodus.

12.line: The redeemed sing praise to the LORD for turning away his anger and becoming their salvation.
more: They will draw water joyfully from the wells of salvation.
They will make his deeds known among the nations.
The Holy One of Israel is great in Zion's midst.

13.line: Isaiah's oracle against Babylon announces the day of the LORD, when the Medes will overthrow the city and leave it desolate.
more: The LORD musters an army from distant lands to destroy the whole land.
Cosmic signs accompany the day of the LORD as he punishes the world's evil.
Babylon will become like Sodom and Gomorrah, inhabited only by wild animals.

14.line: Israel will be restored and mock the fallen king of Babylon, followed by oracles against Assyria and Philistia.
more: The LORD will have compassion on Jacob and settle them in their land.
The king who sought to ascend above God's throne is brought down to Sheol.
The LORD's purpose to break Assyria will stand.
Philistia is warned not to rejoice, for a worse enemy will come.

15.line: An oracle against Moab describes its cities ruined overnight and its people wailing, with the prophet grieving for them.
more: Ar and Kir of Moab are laid waste in a night.
Moabites shave their heads and weep at the high places.
Fugitives flee as the waters dry up and the land fills with blood.

16.line: Moab is urged to seek refuge with Judah's throne, and its pride brings mourning, with judgment set within three years.
more: A throne established in steadfast love will arise in David's tent.
Moab's pride and arrogance are the cause of its downfall.
The prophet weeps over Moab's ruined vineyards.
Within three years Moab's glory will be brought into contempt.

17.line: Damascus and Ephraim will be ruined, people will turn to their Maker, and the raging nations will be rebuked.
more: Damascus will cease to be a city, and Israel's glory will fade.
Only a few will remain, like gleanings after harvest.
Because they forgot the God of their salvation, their plantings will fail.
The nations roar like waters but flee when God rebukes them.

18.line: An oracle addresses Cush, describing how the LORD will cut down its forces and later receive its gifts at Zion.
more: Swift messengers are sent to a tall and smooth-skinned people.
The LORD waits quietly, then prunes the shoots before harvest.
Gifts will be brought to Mount Zion from that people.

19.line: Egypt will suffer civil war, a harsh ruler, and economic collapse, yet will later turn to the LORD alongside Assyria and Israel.
more: The LORD rides to Egypt, and its idols tremble.
The Nile dries up, and Pharaoh's counselors give foolish advice.
An altar to the LORD will stand in Egypt, and Egyptians will worship him.
Israel will be a blessing with Egypt and Assyria in the earth.

20.line: Isaiah walks naked and barefoot for three years as a sign that Assyria will lead Egypt and Cush into captivity.
more: The sign follows Assyria's capture of Ashdod.
Those who trusted Egypt and Cush for help will be ashamed.
The coastland's people will ask how they can escape.

21.line: Oracles announce Babylon's fall, distress for Dumah, and judgment on Arabia within a year.
more: The prophet is distressed by the harsh vision.
A watchman reports that Babylon has fallen and its idols are shattered.
Dumah's watchman is asked how much of the night remains.
Kedar's glory will end and its archers will be few.

22.line: An oracle rebukes Jerusalem for reveling instead of repenting during siege, and Shebna the steward is replaced by Eliakim.
more: The city strengthens its walls and water supply but ignores its Maker.
When called to weeping, they choose feasting, saying tomorrow they die.
Shebna will be hurled away, and Eliakim will receive the key of David's house.
Eliakim will be like a secure peg that eventually gives way.

23.line: An oracle against Tyre announces the fall of the great trading city, its seventy years of being forgotten, and its restoration.
more: Ships of Tarshish and Sidon wail over Tyre's destruction.
The LORD of hosts planned it to dishonor the pride of all glory.
After seventy years Tyre will trade again, and its profits will be holy to the LORD.

24.line: The LORD will lay waste the whole earth because its people broke his covenant, then reign on Mount Zion.
more: Judgment falls on all classes of people alike.
The earth is defiled by its inhabitants and lies under a curse.
A remnant sings praises from the ends of the earth.
The LORD will punish heavenly powers and earthly kings.

25.line: Isaiah praises God for his deliverance and foresees a feast on Mount Zion where death is swallowed up forever.
more: God has been a stronghold to the poor and needy.
The LORD will wipe away tears from all faces.
His people will rejoice in his salvation, while proud Moab is brought low.

26.line: Judah sings of trust in the LORD as an everlasting rock, longs for his judgments, and is promised resurrection.
more: God keeps in perfect peace the one whose mind is fixed on him.
The people confess their own labor brought no deliverance.
Their dead will live, and the earth will give up its dead.
God's people are told to hide briefly until his wrath passes.

27.line: The LORD will slay Leviathan, guard his fruitful vineyard Israel, and gather his scattered people to worship in Jerusalem.
more: Israel will take root and fill the world with fruit.
Jacob's guilt will be atoned when altars and Asherah poles are destroyed.
The fortified city will be left desolate.
A great trumpet will call exiles home from Assyria and Egypt.

28.line: Woe is pronounced on Ephraim's drunken leaders and on Jerusalem's scoffers, but God lays a tested cornerstone in Zion.
more: Samaria's proud crown will be trampled like a fading flower.
Priests and prophets reel with wine and mock the prophet's teaching.
Jerusalem's covenant with death will not stand against the overwhelming scourge.
The New Testament applies the cornerstone to Christ.

29.line: Jerusalem, called Ariel, will be besieged and then suddenly delivered, but its people's hypocrisy blinds them.
more: Its enemies will vanish like a dream.
The people honor God with their lips while their hearts are far from him.
The clay cannot question the potter.
The deaf will hear, the blind will see, and Jacob will no longer be ashamed.

30.line: Judah is rebuked for seeking an alliance with Egypt, yet the LORD waits to be gracious and will shatter Assyria.
more: Egypt's help is worthless and will bring shame.
The people want only pleasant prophecies, refusing quiet trust in the Holy One.
God will answer their cry, guide them, and heal their wounds.
Assyria will be terrified at the LORD's voice and burned like Topheth.

31.line: Woe is pronounced on those who rely on Egypt's horses, for the LORD himself will defend Jerusalem and break Assyria.
more: The Egyptians are men, not God, and their horses are flesh.
The LORD will protect Jerusalem like hovering birds.
Israel is called to return to him and discard their idols.
Assyria will fall by a sword not of man.

32.line: A righteous king will reign and true discernment return, complacent women are warned, and the Spirit will bring lasting peace.
more: Fools will no longer be called noble.
The complacent women of Jerusalem will mourn when the harvest fails.
When the Spirit is poured out, justice and righteousness will produce quietness and trust.

33.line: Woe falls on the destroyer, as the LORD rises to save Zion, where his people will see the King in beauty.
more: The people pray for grace as the land mourns.
Only the righteous can dwell with the consuming fire.
Jerusalem will be a quiet habitation, and its people forgiven.

34.line: The LORD's fury will fall on all nations, with Edom singled out for total and lasting desolation.
more: The armies of the nations will be slaughtered and the heavens rolled up.
Edom's land will burn and become home to wild creatures.
The book of the LORD confirms none of these creatures will be missing.

35.line: The desert will bloom, the weak will be strengthened, and the redeemed will return to Zion on the Way of Holiness.
more: The glory of the LORD will be seen in the wilderness.
The blind will see, the deaf hear, and the lame leap.
The ransomed will come with singing, and sorrow will flee.

36.line: Sennacherib's field commander besieges Jerusalem and taunts Hezekiah's people, claiming neither Egypt nor the LORD can save them.
more: Assyria has already captured Judah's fortified cities.
The Rabshakeh speaks in Hebrew so the people on the wall understand.
The people stay silent, and the officials report to Hezekiah with torn clothes.

37.line: Hezekiah prays, Isaiah announces God's answer, and the angel of the LORD strikes down 185,000 Assyrians.
more: Hezekiah seeks Isaiah, who says the Assyrian king will return home.
After a threatening letter, Hezekiah spreads it before the LORD in prayer.
Isaiah's oracle rebukes Sennacherib's pride and promises Jerusalem's defense.
Sennacherib withdraws to Nineveh, where his sons kill him.

38.line: Hezekiah falls mortally ill, prays, and receives fifteen more years, confirmed by the shadow moving backward on the steps.
more: Isaiah first tells him to set his house in order.
The LORD also promises to defend Jerusalem from Assyria.
Hezekiah writes a psalm of thanks for his recovery.
Isaiah prescribes a fig poultice for his boil.

39.line: Hezekiah shows Babylonian envoys all his treasures, and Isaiah predicts everything will be carried off to Babylon.
more: Merodach-baladan sends envoys after Hezekiah's recovery.
Some of Hezekiah's descendants will serve in Babylon's palace.
Hezekiah accepts the word, relieved there will be peace in his days.

40.line: God commands comfort for Jerusalem, announces his coming, and declares his incomparable power to strengthen the weary.
more: A voice cries to prepare the LORD's way in the wilderness.
The Gospels apply the wilderness voice to John the Baptist.
No idol compares to the Creator who measures the heavens.
Those who wait for the LORD will renew their strength.

41.line: The LORD challenges the nations and their idols, raising a conqueror and assuring Israel, his servant, of his help.
more: God stirs up one from the east who tramples kings.
Israel should not fear, for God will strengthen and uphold them.
He will turn deserts into pools for the poor and needy.
The idols are summoned to predict the future and proven worthless.

42.line: The LORD presents his Servant who will bring justice gently to the nations, then rebukes blind and deaf Israel.
more: God puts his Spirit on the Servant, who will not break a bruised reed.
Matthew applies this Servant passage to Jesus.
A new song praises the LORD going forth like a warrior.
Israel was given to plunder because they would not obey.

43.line: The LORD promises to redeem and gather Israel, declares himself the only Savior, and announces a new thing.
more: Israel need not fear, for God is with them through waters and fire.
Israel are his witnesses that there is no god besides him.
He will make a way in the wilderness for his people.
Though Israel wearied God with sins, he blots out their transgressions.

44.line: The LORD pours his Spirit on Israel, exposes the folly of idol-making, and names Cyrus to rebuild Jerusalem.
more: The LORD is the first and the last, and there is no other God.
A craftsman burns half a log for fire and worships the other half.
Israel is called to return, for God has redeemed them.
Cyrus is called God's shepherd, who will order the temple rebuilt.

45.line: The LORD anoints Cyrus for Israel's sake and calls all the ends of the earth to turn and be saved.
more: God will open doors before Cyrus, though Cyrus does not know him.
God forms light and darkness and is sovereign over all.
The clay should not argue with its potter.
Every knee will bow and every tongue swear allegiance to the LORD.

46.line: Babylon's idols must be carried as burdens, but the LORD carries his people from birth to old age.
more: Bel and Nebo bow down and go into captivity.
No idol can save those who cry to it.
God declares the end from the beginning and will accomplish his purpose.
He will call a bird of prey from the east.

47.line: Virgin daughter Babylon will be humbled from queen to slave for her cruelty, pride, and sorceries.
more: Babylon showed no mercy to God's people when he handed them over.
She boasted she would never be a widow or lose children.
Her enchantments and astrologers cannot save her.

48.line: The LORD rebukes stubborn Israel, explains why he foretold events, and calls his people to flee from Babylon.
more: God announced things beforehand so Israel could not credit idols.
He refined them in the furnace of affliction for his own name's sake.
Had they obeyed, their peace would have been like a river.
There is no peace for the wicked.

49.line: The Servant will restore Israel and be a light to the nations, and the LORD assures Zion he has not forgotten her.
more: The Servant was called from the womb and made like a sharpened sword.
Kings will bow, and captives will be freed.
A mother may forget her child, but God will not forget Zion.
Zion's children will return in such numbers that the land seems too small.

50.line: Israel's exile came from its sins, and the obedient Servant endures abuse while trusting God to vindicate him.
more: The LORD did not divorce Israel; their sins sent them away.
The Servant gave his back to those who struck him and did not hide from spitting.
He sets his face like flint, sure the Lord will help him.
Those who walk in darkness should trust in the LORD's name.

51.line: The LORD calls the faithful to look to Abraham, promises lasting salvation, and summons Jerusalem to awake from his wrath.
more: God will comfort Zion and make her wilderness like Eden.
His salvation will last forever, though the heavens vanish.
The arm that dried the sea will bring the ransomed to Zion.
The cup of wrath is taken from Jerusalem and given to her tormentors.

52.line: Zion is called to awake and rejoice as the LORD returns and redeems her, and his Servant will be exalted.
more: Jerusalem was sold for nothing and will be redeemed without money.
Beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news.
The people are told to depart and touch no unclean thing.
The Servant's appearance is marred beyond human likeness, yet he will startle many nations.

53.line: The Servant, despised and rejected, bears his people's sins and dies as an offering, then is exalted and justifies many.
more: He was wounded for others' transgressions, and by his wounds they are healed.
Like a lamb led to slaughter, he was silent before his oppressors.
Though buried with the wicked, he will see offspring and prolong his days.
The New Testament applies this chapter to Christ's suffering and death.

54.line: The LORD calls barren Zion to sing, for he will enlarge her family and keep his covenant of peace forever.
more: Her Maker is her husband, who will gather her with great compassion.
His covenant of peace will not be removed, like his oath to Noah.
Jerusalem will be rebuilt with precious stones, and no weapon against her will succeed.

55.line: The LORD invites all who thirst to come freely, seek him while he may be found, and receive his everlasting covenant.
more: He promises his steadfast love for David in an everlasting covenant.
The wicked should forsake their ways and return for abundant pardon.
God's thoughts and ways are higher than human ones.
His word will not return empty but will accomplish his purpose.

56.line: The LORD promises blessing to foreigners and eunuchs who keep his covenant, and rebukes Israel's greedy, blind leaders.
more: Those who keep justice and the Sabbath are blessed.
His house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples.
Israel's watchmen are like silent dogs and greedy shepherds.

57.line: The righteous perish unnoticed, idolaters are exposed and condemned, but the LORD revives the humble and contrite.
more: The idolaters practice pagan sexual rites and child sacrifice.
Their collection of idols cannot deliver them.
The high and holy God dwells with the lowly in spirit.
There is no peace for the wicked.

58.line: The LORD rejects Israel's self-serving fasts and describes the true fast of justice, compassion, and honoring the Sabbath.
more: They fast while oppressing workers and quarreling.
True fasting frees the oppressed, feeds the hungry, and clothes the naked.
Then their light will break forth, and the LORD will guide them.
Delighting in the Sabbath will bring joy in the LORD.

59.line: Israel's sins have separated them from God, but seeing no one to intervene, the LORD himself brings salvation.
more: Their hands are stained with blood and their tongues speak lies.
The people confess that justice is far from them.
The LORD puts on righteousness as armor and repays his enemies.
A Redeemer will come to Zion, and God's Spirit and words will remain.

60.line: Zion's light has come, and nations will bring their wealth to her as the LORD becomes her everlasting light.
more: Kings and nations will come to the brightness of her rising.
Foreigners will rebuild her walls, and her gates will always be open.
Violence will no longer be heard in her land.
The sun and moon will be unnecessary, for the LORD is her light.

61.line: The anointed one proclaims good news to the afflicted, freedom to captives, and the LORD's favor, bringing joy to Zion.
more: Mourners receive beauty instead of ashes and garments of praise.
They will rebuild ancient ruins and be called priests of the LORD.
Jesus read this passage in Nazareth and declared it fulfilled.
Zion rejoices, clothed in garments of salvation.

62.line: The LORD will not rest until Jerusalem's righteousness shines, and he gives her a new name as his delight.
more: She will no longer be called Forsaken but Hephzibah and Married.
Watchmen are set on her walls to pray continually.
Her people will be called the Holy People, the Redeemed of the LORD.

63.line: The LORD returns from Edom in blood-stained garments after judging the nations, and Isaiah recalls his mercies and pleads for help.
more: He trod the winepress of wrath alone.
Isaiah recounts the LORD's steadfast love and Israel's grieving of his Holy Spirit.
He recalls how God led them through the sea by Moses.
He asks God to look down, for he is their Father and Redeemer.

64.line: Isaiah prays for God to come down in power, confesses Israel's sin, and appeals to him as Father and potter.
more: No eye has seen a God like him, who acts for those who wait.
All their righteous deeds are like a polluted garment.
Zion is a wilderness and the temple burned, so he asks God not to stay silent.

65.line: The LORD answers that he will judge rebellious idolaters but spare a remnant, and he will create new heavens and earth.
more: He held out his hands to a rebellious people who provoked him.
His servants will eat and rejoice while the rebels hunger and are ashamed.
Jerusalem will be a joy, with long life and no weeping.
The wolf and lamb will feed together on his holy mountain.

66.line: The LORD seeks humble worshipers, promises Zion's sudden rebirth, and announces judgment on the wicked and the gathering of all nations.
more: Heaven is his throne, and he values the contrite over sacrifice.
Zion will give birth to a nation in a day, and God will comfort her like a mother.
Nations will see his glory, and some will be sent to declare it.
The new heavens and earth will endure, while rebels face unending judgment.
